definition: How much a component opposes the current in it: the p.d. across it divided by the current, $R = \frac{V}{I}$, measured in ohms ($\Omega$).
A component made to have a fixed resistance; at constant temperature the current in it is directly proportional to the p.d. across it.
The current in a metal conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across it, as long as its temperature stays the same.
A lamp with a thin metal wire (the filament) that glows when hot; its resistance increases as it gets hotter, so its current–voltage graph (current on the vertical axis) gets less steep.
A component that lets current flow in one direction only: it has a low resistance in the forward direction and a very high resistance in reverse.

For wires of the same metal at the same temperature, a longer wire (same thickness) has more resistance and a thicker wire (same length) less (Extended: $R$ is directly proportional to length for the same area, and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area for the same length).
